clue.text: Discard cigarette-end in grate

parts.note: to discard something is to scrap it

indicators.note: the end of the word cigarette is its final letter

explanation.surface: A smoker throws the stub of a cigarette into the fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grate' looks like the fireplace of the surface, but it is the verb: to grate is to rasp.
explanation.definitionFit: To grate and to scrape both mean to rub harshly against a surface.

clue.text: Subsidiary interest in E Indies lake resort

indicators.note: to re-sort is to sort again, so these letters are put in a fresh order

parts.note: L is an abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: Someone with a side business at a lakeside holiday spot in the East Indies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resort' looks like a holiday place but is read as re-sort, rearranging E INDIES with L.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideline is a secondary occupation or line of business pursued alongside the main one.

clue.text: Points in circular are much talked about

indicators.note: in places the points inside the word for circular

parts.note: round means circular
E and S are compass points, east and south

explanation.surface: Points in a circular letter become the talk of the town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circular' looks like a leaflet but is the adjective round.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that resound echo widely, so they are celebrated and much discussed.

clue.text: Do the consumer's work for him

definitions.text: Do the consumer's work for him

parts.words: Do the consumer's work for him
parts.note: breaking food down in advance so the eater's stomach has less to do

explanation.definitionFit: Treating food so it is partly broken down before eating spares the stomach its digestive labour.

clue.text: Not penalised, being tax-exempt

parts.note: scot is an old word for a tax or levy
exempt means free of an obligation

explanation.surface: Someone escapes punishment because their income is not taxed.
explanation.walkthrough: SCOT, an archaic tax, gives the phrase its origin: getting off without paying the levy.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting off without punishment or harm is going unscathed in an idiom of escape.

clue.text: Schoolchildren lined up with careers? Good grief, no!

parts.note: a crocodile is a British term for schoolchildren walking in a line of pairs
to career is to rush along, as does one who tears

explanation.surface: Pupils in a line rushing about, and someone saying it is no cause for sorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a crocodile is a line of schoolchildren walking in pairs. 'careers' looks like jobs but is the verb meaning rushes.
explanation.definitionFit: Insincere weeping shows grief that is not real, as the definition's exclamation denies it.

clue.text: Trunk too big? Rubbish — it's on the way up

indicators.note: in a down entry, on the way up means the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, too big for standard sizes
rot means nonsense, rubbish

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses the claim that a tree trunk is oversized, noting it grows upward.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the way up' turns OS + ROT backwards. 'Trunk' looks like a tree but is the body's torso sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The trunk is the human body without head and limbs, its central part.

clue.text: Bat — more than one needed for a game

definitions.meaning: a bat used to strike a ball in tennis or squash

definitions.text: more than one needed for a game
definitions.meaning: the plural names the court game rackets, played with these bats

explanation.surface: A bat, and players need several to make up a game.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural is the name of the old court game, so 'more than one' makes the game.
explanation.definitionFit: A strung bat for hitting balls is this item, and its plural names the court game racquets.

clue.text: Corrects boundaries round state

indicators.note: round says the boundaries' word goes around the state

parts.note: ends are boundaries or limits
ME is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Maine

explanation.surface: Someone redraws the borders surrounding a state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state' gives ME, the abbreviation for Maine.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend is to remove errors from a text, revising it.

clue.text: Wet suit?

parts.note: not the diver's rubber suit but any garment worn to go swimming

explanation.definitionFit: Clothing worn to swim gets wet, so a swimsuit is a suit for wet conditions.

clue.text: Does padre reform the criminal? Yes

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters of these two words are reshaped

explanation.surface: A question whether a priest can redeem a lawbreaker, answered with a cheerful yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reform' reads as moral redemption, which suits a padre, but it signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless outlaw, a violent criminal of the Wild West kind.

clue.text: Strip of lawn, perhaps, for shrub outside the church

indicators.note: the shrub's letters go round the outside of the church's abbreviation

parts.note: rue is a bitter-leaved herb grown as a small shrub
CH is the usual abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A gardener's note about a strip of grass and a bush beyond the churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: Lawn here is the fine linen fabric, not grass; 'perhaps' marks it as one example of material a frill is made from.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruche is a gathered frill of fabric, and lawn is one fine cloth used for it.

clue.text: Should one translate this volume?

indicators.note: to translate is to render in other terms, so the letters of the word are rendered anew

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one

explanation.surface: A publisher wonders whether a certain book ought to be translated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translate' rearranges SHOULD with I. 'volume' looks like a book, but it is a level of sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A fairly loud level of sound is one setting of volume on a dial.

clue.text: Not dour, perhaps, but pompous

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the words might be arranged differently, so their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is described as not sullen but rather self-important.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface contrasts two characters, but 'Not dour' is simply the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Orotund describes a style of speech that is grandiose and self-important.

clue.text: Jog to attract attention

parts.note: a light prod with the elbow given to make someone notice something

explanation.definitionFit: A gentle push with the elbow is the gesture used to catch someone's notice.

clue.text: No single fixed note in this part of Tchaikovsky's suite

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral I is one, a single
set means fixed or firm
te is the seventh note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A music critic notes that one passage of a Tchaikovsky suite has no sustained single note.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nutcracker is 'Casse-Noisette' in French, so the answer forms part of the suite's French title.
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker Suite is titled Casse-Noisette in French, so this word is one component of that name.

clue.text: F. or say T. almost complete a difficult word

indicators.note: say asks for the letter and word before it to be spoken aloud, their sound giving a spelling

parts.note: the letter F said as ef, followed by or
the letter T, taken as written

indicators.note: almost means the word falls short by its final letter

parts.note: full means complete

explanation.surface: A grammarian ponders whether F or T can finish an awkward word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' asks for 'F. or' spoken: ef-or, then T follows. 'almost' drops the last L from FULL. 'a' and 'word' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Effortful describes work demanding great exertion, hence hard to do.

clue.text: Girls who marry out of honour are boring people

indicators.note: out of means outside of, so the brides go round the honour

parts.note: brides are women getting married
OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Women who wed only out of a sense of duty turn out to be dull company.
explanation.walkthrough: OM, the Order of Merit, is a British honour. 'out of' reads as motive but means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: A bromide, once a sedative, came to mean a tiresome, platitudinous person.

clue.text: This hymn may cause laughter to be heard

indicators.note: to be heard tells the solver the phrase is spoken, its sound giving a different spelling

parts.note: can tickle means is able to amuse, and so may raise a laugh

explanation.surface: A hymn so funny it sets the congregation giggling.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, 'can tickle' gives the sound of the church song's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A canticle is a song or chant with a biblical text sung in church services.

clue.text: Made suit — fitted too!

explanation.surface: A tailor makes a suit and it is fitted as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made suit' reads as tailoring but means made suitable.
explanation.definitionFit: Something altered to suit a purpose has been modified, so both senses describe adjustment.

clue.text: Thighbone found in wife murder case

indicators.note: found in says the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Forensic evidence turns up in the investigation of a woman's killing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' completes the courtroom picture and works with 'found in' as a link to the run 'wife murder'.
explanation.definitionFit: The femur is the long bone running from hip to knee in the upper leg.

clue.text: Brindled cat up the West End showed the way

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the cat is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a tom is a male cat

indicators.note: end picks the final letter of the word West

parts.note: to lead is to show the way, past tense led

explanation.surface: A streaky cat climbs up and guides people through London's theatre district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the West End' looks like London's theatre district, but 'End' picks the last letter of West.
explanation.definitionFit: Brindled means streaked or patched with darker colour, so blotchy in appearance.

clue.text: Fight Sarah at the card table

definitions.meaning: Sarah, the whist-loving old lady of a Charles Lamb essay about her opinions on whist

explanation.surface: A woman named Sarah squabbles over cards.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Lamb's essay on a whist-loving old lady, Mrs ... Opinions on Whist, gives Sarah her surname.
explanation.definitionFit: A fight is a combat, and Lamb's devoted whist player Sarah bore this surname.

clue.text: Newfoundland nurse rebuffed one as a liar

indicators.note: rebuffed suggests being pushed back, so the nurse's name is read backwards

parts.note: Nana, the Darling children's nursemaid in Peter Pan, is a Newfoundland dog
the Roman numeral I is one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog-nurse spurns someone she regards as a fibber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newfoundland' looks like the Canadian province, but it is the dog breed of Nana in Peter Pan; her name backwards is ANAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ananias was struck dead in Acts for lying, so his name became a byword for a deceiver.

clue.text: Thessalonian who became a permanent revolutionary

definitions.text: Thessalonian who became a permanent revolutionary

parts.words: Thessalonian who became a permanent revolutionary
parts.note: a king of Thessaly bound by Zeus to a fiery wheel that turns forever

explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this Lapith king was tied to an eternally spinning wheel in punishment.

clue.text: Offend a corporation by written mistake

parts.note: to err is to sin or offend
corporation is an old jocular word for a pot belly, a tum

explanation.surface: A complaint about upsetting a company through some error on paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporation' looks like a company, but it is old slang for a large stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: An erratum is an error in print or writing, listed in a correction slip.

clue.text: Half an ice-cream for the whole orchestra!

indicators.note: half says only the first of the two equal parts of the ice cream's name is used

parts.note: the ice cream with mixed candied fruit has a two-part rhyming Italian name

explanation.surface: Someone shares half an ice cream with every member of the orchestra.
explanation.walkthrough: The ice cream is never named; solvers must think of the fruit-studded Italian kind with a doubled name and keep its front half.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutti is the Italian musical direction meaning all performers play together.

clue.text: A Continental played first, captured a trump, and collected

indicators.note: captured means holding something inside, so the trump goes within the other letters

parts.note: un is French for a, as a Continental would say
in card games to lead is to play first, so led is played first
to ruff is to play a trump card

explanation.surface: A bridge report: a European led, then took a trick with a trump, and composed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collected' looks like the cards being gathered in, but it means composed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being collected means calm and composed, untroubled by events.

clue.text: Threaten to name grandee in evolution

indicators.note: evolution suggests gradual change in form, so the letters are developed into a new order

explanation.surface: A noble is threatened with being named as the world changes around him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in evolution' rearranges N plus GRANDEE.
explanation.definitionFit: To endanger is to put at risk, which is to threaten harm.

clue.text: Moves easily in the Palais dances

definitions.meaning: a palais de danse is a British public dance hall; slides across its floor are dance steps

explanation.surface: Couples drift smoothly round a public dance hall.
explanation.walkthrough: A palais (palais de danse) was a large public dance hall in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Smooth sliding movements are both effortless travel and steps of dancing in a ballroom.
